title: Scotch Broth
subtitle: Traditional Scottish barley soup with lamb
excerpt: A thick, filling soup of lamb neck, pearl barley, and root vegetables, simmered slowly until the barley swells and the broth is rich and cloudy. Scotland's national soup.

recipe.sourceNotes: Scotch broth is one of the oldest recorded soups in British cooking. Early versions from the 17th and 18th centuries used whatever meat was available, most commonly mutton or lamb, along with whatever dried pulses and root vegetables were in store. The pearl barley is the defining ingredient: it thickens the broth as it cooks, releasing starch into the liquid. The soup is better the next day after the barley has continued to swell overnight. It is traditionally served as a meal in itself with bread, not as a starter. The lamb neck is ideal because it is inexpensive, gelatinous, and flavourful, though lamb shoulder or mutton can be substituted.

content.text: Start with cold water and bring to a boil, skimming off the grey foam that rises in the first few minutes: this gives a clearer broth. The barley goes in early as it needs the full cooking time to soften and swell. The vegetables go in later so they do not disintegrate completely. Taste for seasoning at the end: the salt level depends on how salty your stock or water is.
Place the lamb in a large pot and cover with 2 litres of cold water. Bring to a boil. Skim off all the grey foam that rises to the surface. Add the bay leaves and thyme.
Add the barley, onion, carrot, and swede. Return to a gentle simmer. Cook partially covered for 1 hour 30 minutes.

Remove the lamb. Pull the meat from the bones and return it to the pot. Discard the bones, bay leaves, and thyme. Add the leek and celery. Simmer for a further 20 minutes until the leek is tender. Season with salt and pepper. Stir in the parsley and serve.
